items.title: Romanian Dental Students’ Usage, Trust, and Attitudes Toward Generative AI: A Cross-Sectional Survey
items.abstract: Background/Objectives: Evidence on how Romanian dental students use generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is limited. This study assessed academic GenAI use, perceived educational and clinical usefulness, self-reported trust, ethical concerns, and attitudes toward curricular integration and institutional guidance. Methods: A cross-sectional paper-based survey was administered on 12 and 13 February 2026 to fourth- and fifth-year dental students attending scheduled teaching activities at one Romanian university. Of 192 eligible students, 167 attended the recruitment sessions, 155 responded (92.8%), and 148 were analysed. The study-specific questionnaire underwent expert content review but not psychometric validation. Spearman correlations, the Wilcoxon signed-rank test, and a supplementary chi-square test were applied with Holm correction across 18 tests; open-ended answers underwent descriptive thematic analysis. Results: Overall, 41.2% of students used GenAI frequently or very frequently. Use frequency correlated weakly to moderately with perceived understanding, time-saving, academic performance, and educational value (ρ = 0.25–0.51). ChatGPT received higher usefulness ratings for learning dental concepts than AI in general received for clinical decision-making (median 4 vs. 3; p < 0.001), although the items referred to different AI applications. Trust correlated moderately with perceived educational value (ρ = 0.49). Privacy and critical-thinking concerns correlated moderately with support for institutional guidelines (ρ = 0.36 and 0.46), whereas critical-thinking concern was unrelated to support for curricular integration. Conclusions: Students regarded GenAI mainly as an educational aid and were cautious about its clinical use. Structured training in critical appraisal and ethical use, supported by institutional policy, appears warranted. The associations are cross-sectional and may not generalise beyond this sample.

items.title: Safeguards, residual failures, and human oversight in clinical agentic and related artificial intelligence workflows: a systematic scoping review
items.abstract: Background Clinical agentic artificial intelligence (AI) can alter its actions during a clinical task, creating failure pathways that conventional performance metrics may not capture. Whether safeguards interrupt these pathways remains uncertain. Aim To map safeguard effects, residual failures, human recovery, and resource consequences in clinical agentic and related AI workflows. Methods We searched PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, Scopus, Web of Science Core Collection, and IEEE Xplore, for English-language, peer-reviewed empirical journal reports. This scoping review used independent screening, duplicate extraction, narrative synthesis, and result-specific critical appraisal. Results The 111 reports comprised 56 functionally agentic, 29 related non-agentic, 22 architecture-uncertain, and four human-factors reports; 38 of the 56 agentic reports explicitly documented model-directed subsequent-action selection. Among the 111 selected appraisal results, none both isolated a specified safeguard’s effect and demonstrated reduced measured patient harm. Configurations incorporating safeguards improved selected outcomes, but gains coexisted with omissions, reduced sensitivity, false reassurance, delay, or transferred review burden. Concurrent changes in models, prompts, evidence access, and workflow frequently prevented attribution to individual controls. Some patient-randomised trials reported patient or process benefits, but evaluated bundled interventions rather than the contribution of a safeguard. Human authority was more often documented than successful error detection and recovery; requiring clinician approval did not establish that residual errors were recognised and corrected. Performance varied across models, settings, and information conditions, limiting transfer of favourable findings. Reported efficiency gains depended on measurement boundaries and did not consistently account for review, correction, escalation, and downstream work. Discussion The evidence exposes a gap between local error control and safety across a complete clinical episode. A safeguard can reduce a targeted error while shifting risk to later decisions or human reviewers. We propose a post hoc , non-ordinal evidence profile addressing mechanism fidelity, residual and introduced failures, robustness, joint human–AI performance, and clinical consequences. The profile requires validation; heterogeneous designs and retrospective methodological refinements constrain inference. Conclusion Clinical safety should be evaluated across the complete care pathway, tracing safeguard effects through residual error, human recovery, and patient-relevant outcomes. Selective autonomy requires joint assessment of residual risk and the capacity for timely human review.

items.title: Safety Training and Health-Seeking Behaviour among Oil and Gas Dispensing Workers: Evidence from a Cross-Sectional Study in Calabar Metropolis, Nigeria
items.abstract: Occupational health risks are common among oil and gas dispensing workers, making safety training an important component of workplace health protection. This study examined the relationship between safety training and health-seeking behaviour among oil and gas dispensing workers in Calabar Metropolis, Cross River State, Nigeria. A cross-sectional research design was adopted, and data were collected from 212 oil and gas dispensing workers using a structured questionnaire. Safety training and health-seeking behaviour were measured using composite scores derived from Likert-type items. Descriptive statistics were used to assess the extent of safety training practices, while Pearson Product Moment Correlation and simple linear regression were employed to examine the relationship and predictive effect of safety training on health-seeking behaviour. The findings indicated a high level of safety training among the workers. A strong, positive and statistically significant relationship was found between safety training and health-seeking behaviour (r = .775, p < .001). Regression analysis further showed that safety training significantly and positively predicted health-seeking behaviour (B = 0.685, β = .776, t = 17.842, p < .001). The regression model was statistically significant, F(1, 210) = 318.354, p < .001, and explained 60.3% of the variance in health-seeking behaviour (R² = .603). The study concludes that higher levels of safety training are associated with more positive health-seeking behaviour among oil and gas dispensing workers. It recommends sustained and periodic safety training incorporating hazard recognition, preventive health practices, early reporting of health problems and appropriate utilisation of healthcare services. Practically, the study provides evidence for integrating health-seeking components into routine safety training, particularly early recognition and reporting of occupational health problems, preventive practices, and appropriate utilisation of healthcare services. Keywords: Safety training; Health-seeking behaviour; Occupational health; oil and gas workers; Calabar Metropolis.

items.title: ScreenRecompose: Semantic-Aware Generative Content Replacement for Privacy Protection in Screen Sharing
items.abstract: Screen sharing in online conferencing can unintentionally expose private information on the presenter’s screen. Existing protections mainly rely on masking or blurring, which can disrupt context and interaction understanding. We propose a generative, semantic-aware replacement approach that substitutes sensitive regions with visually coherent content in dynamic screen environments. We implement two variants with different degrees of semantic grounding: Semantic-Element-Preserving Replacement (SEPR) and Semantic-Element-Agnostic Replacement (SEAR), and compare them with masking and blurring. In a video-based user study that isolates latency effects, we evaluate detectability, confidence of detection, perceived identifiability, and user experience from both screen-sharer and screen-viewer perspectives. SEAR significantly reduced detectability relative to masking, and also lowered perceived identifiability compared to blurring and SEPR. Replacement methods significantly improved context understanding and visual naturalness over masking, and SEAR also outperformed blurring in visual naturalness; for context preservation, SEAR was rated higher than masking, while the SEPR–masking comparison was near the significance threshold. Qualitative responses further revealed role-dependent concerns and a social risk of misinterpretation, motivating design implications for tuning semantic fidelity and signaling obfuscation intent.

items.title: Securing Collaborative Data Ecosystems: A Sociotechnical Framework for Mitigating Insider Risk and Governance Fail-ures in Inter Organizational Information Systems
items.abstract: The use of inter-organizational information systems (such as cloud computing environments, data markets and sup-ply chains) provides organizations with the ability to manage their activities together and generate value from those shared activities. However, while technical controls are important to limit the spread of damage caused by unauthor-ized actions taken by employees within the organization, technical controls cannot prevent the consequences of em-ployees acting outside of established policies or the absence of effective organizational governance. A single over-permissive policy or configuration error can affect multiple organizations that are part of the same network and lead to loss of trust among those organizations and non-compliance with regulations. To address the need for a compre-hensive sociotechnical framework for understanding how behavior, technical controls and institutional governance influence the exposure of organizations to risk, we developed the Collaborative Security Alignment (CSA) model based upon Orlikowski's duality of technology, Protection Motivation Theory and Task-Technology Fit. The CSA model proposes that: (a) Technical controls are a prerequisite for protecting organization resources but are not suffi-cient; (b) Organizational culture and behavioral nudges influence the effectiveness of technical controls; and (c) Inter-organizational governance (via contracts, auditing and common metrics) contributes to long-term resiliency. We used a convergent mixed methods approach to assess the validity of the CSA model. We conducted a survey of 210 IS professionals and analyzed the data using Structural Equation Modeling (SEM); we completed three case studies and analyzed them using thematic analysis; and we created a novel, reproducible simulation that compares a rule-based baseline to a CSA toolkit consisting of machine learning-based anomaly detection, workflow-embedded policy nudges, tiered access governance, and shared auditing. Our SEM analysis supported each of our four hypoth-eses. Our simulation results indicated that when all components of the CSA toolkit were applied collectively, the aggregate exposure to vulnerabilities was reduced by approximately 67 percent compared to the baseline (range of sectors was 56-80%). Since the reduction in exposure to vulnerability is dependent on the assumptions made con-cerning the effects of each component of the CSA toolkit, we provide ablation and sensitivity analyses (results var-ied from 58-75 percent across the tested ranges) and consider the findings as a demonstration of the model's capabil-ities as opposed to empirical evidence. We conclude our paper with recommendations for managers and discussions of algorithmic fairness, ethical considerations related to conducting research and cross-jurisdictional regulatory compliance issues.

items.title: Seeing inside AI Agents: How Transparency Shapes Human-Agent Interactions
items.abstract: As Large Language Model (LLM)-based agents increasingly make decisions and take actions for users, understanding how transparency shapes human–agent interaction is critical. We report a controlled study with 60 participants interacting with a policy-governed agent in a customer-service domain under three transparency conditions: opaque, partial, and transparent. The study shows greater transparency increased perceived understanding of agent behavior. However, it did not improve identification of silent failures, defined as plausible errors presented without warning. Partial transparency supported error detection more effectively than full transparency, suggesting that additional explanations do not necessarily enhance critical evaluation. Greater transparency was also associated with lower perceived agent steerability, reflecting reduced belief that outcomes could be influenced through altered response strategies. Participants challenged agent decisions less directly and engaged more with stated rules under transparent conditions. These findings highlight trade-offs between clarity, oversight, and user agency, motivating transparency designs that better support effective human oversight.

items.title: Self-Perceived Academic Artificial Intelligence Overreliance Associated with Academic Performance Among Nursing Students in a Resource-Limited Setting: A Multicentre, Cross- Sectional—Correlational Study
items.abstract: Background Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is embedded in nursing students' routines, yet academic AI overreliance is rarely quantified, especially in resource-limited settings. Objective To examine the relationship between self-perceived academic AI overreliance and academic performance among nursing students in the West Bank, Palestine. Methods A multicentre, cross-sectional correlational study was conducted with 1213 second- to fourth-year nursing students from 11 Palestinian universities who completed the 22-item Academic AI Overreliance Scale (AAIO) and the 8-item Academic Performance Scale (AP). The relationship between self-perceived academic AI overreliance and academic performance was estimated using hierarchical regression analysis, with sociodemographic and academic characteristics being entered in the first step, and academic AI overreliance being added in the second step. Results The mean age of participants was 21.79 years (SD = 1.09; range 20–25 years), and 676 of them (55.7%) were female. The self-perceived academic AI overreliance in the study was moderate (mean = 2.42, SD = 0.49). Higher self-perceived academic AI overreliance was associated with higher self-reported academic performance (r = 0.34, p < 0.001); this self-perceived academic AI overreliance was the associated factor (β = 0.35, p < 0.001). Conclusions Self-perceived academic AI overreliance was common yet moderate; its positive association with academic performance underscores the need to shape AI engagement and safeguard unassisted learning. The findings give nurse educators a measurable target for AI-literacy curricula, assessment design and institutional policy in a resource-limited setting.

items.title: Self-reported artificial intelligence familiarity, use, and attitudes among students, faculty, and staff at a medical college in the United Arab Emirates: a cross-sectional survey
items.abstract: Background Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used in healthcare and medical education. We described self-reported AI familiarity, use, and attitudes among students, faculty, and staff at a medical college in the United Arab Emirates to inform local training. Methods We conducted a cross-sectional online survey from August to October 2025. Study-specific composite summary scores ranged from 0 to 100. Linear models adjusted for respondent group, sex, and age, with HC3 standard errors. Sensitivity analyses examined AI use scoring, bootstrap confidence intervals, and restricted-age group comparisons. Results After four blank records were excluded, 375 respondents remained; the estimated participation proportion was 34.7%. At least one use of a generative AI tool during the previous three months was reported by 96.8% of respondents, whereas 78.1% reported AI use specifically in academic studies or professional practice. Formal AI training was reported by 10.8%. Mean AI familiarity, AI use, and AI attitude scores were 61.6, 62.9, and 72.1. Adjusted student-versus-faculty/staff differences were 1.91 points for AI familiarity (95% confidence interval [CI] -6.99 to 10.81), -2.87 for AI use (95% CI -23.17 to 17.43), and 2.32 for AI attitude (95% CI -5.43 to 10.07). Because age overlap between students and faculty/staff was limited, these adjusted group estimates may partly rely on extrapolation and should not be interpreted as age-matched comparisons. Average linear-model age associations indicated lower AI familiarity and higher AI attitude scores. The adjusted male-versus-female AI use estimate was uncertain (-7.61, 95% CI -16.14 to 0.92). The higher adjusted AI attitude score among male respondents was exploratory and requires caution because no multiplicity adjustment was applied. Training-stage comparisons were exploratory and showed no consistent pattern. The restricted-age analysis included 59 respondents and had wide confidence intervals. Conclusions Any recent generative AI use was common, while formal training was uncommon. These findings may guide local teaching on responsible AI use, checking AI-generated information, and maintaining human oversight. Self-report, one institution, and study-specific scores that were not formally validated limit interpretation. Future studies should validate the measures and include objective assessments of AI competency.

items.title: Semantic-Topological Cognitive Maps for Assistive Indoor Navigation of a Robot Partner
items.abstract: Assistive indoor mobile robots are increasingly expected to connect natural-language requests about familiar places and objects with the metric maps used for localization and motion planning. Metric simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM) supports reliable geometry and collision avoidance, whereas many open-vocabulary scene-graph systems remain separated from the navigation stacks used on deployed robots. This paper presents a semantic-topological cognitive map (STCM) that bridges these representations for assistive navigation. The system derives place nodes from a LiDAR–inertial pose stream through a dual growing neural gas backend and consolidates object instances over time. GroundingDINO and MobileSAM provide open-vocabulary semantic grounding in the map frame through LiDAR–image association and temporal score fusion. A tool-mediated large language model interface maps user commands to explicit STCM nodes, while graph search and ROS 2 Navigation2 (Nav2) remain responsible for path computation and execution. Evaluation with recorded robot sessions, an outdoor distribution-shift probe, and a public indoor-scene benchmark indicates that the STCM backend improves object-graph construction and that the language interface improves functional-command grounding when requested objects are recoverable by perception. The pipeline is demonstrated on a Ranger Garden Assistant platform with FAST-LIO2 mapping, incremental graph construction during the mapping pass, and waypoint execution from a serialized map artifact.

items.title: Senior phase educators’ perceptions of artificial intelligence tools in geometry: A South African case study
items.abstract: Geometry education in South Africa’s Senior Phase has been marked by low learner attainment and a disconnect between the potential of artificial intelligence (AI) tools and their classroom use. Despite global advances, educators’ readiness to integrate AI in this context has remained underexplored. This study examined Senior Phase mathematics educators’ perceptions of integrating AI tools into geometry teaching. It focused on perceived benefits, implementation barriers, and the role of professional development in enabling meaningful use. A qualitative case study design was employed within a constructivist paradigm. Nine purposively selected educators from urban schools in the Free State and Gauteng participated in semi-structured interviews. Data were analysed thematically using a hybrid deductive–inductive approach. Educators showed cautious optimism, identifying improved visualisation, time efficiency, and support for differentiated learning. However, implementation was constrained by infrastructural instability, limited device access, curriculum pressures, and lack of subject-specific training. The use of AI remained largely confined to lesson preparation, and concerns about cognitive surrender emerged. The findings indicated that AI integration was constrained less by technology than by systemic and pedagogical limitations. Professional development emerged as the decisive factor shaping classroom use. Artificial intelligence was also identified as enabling educator inclusion in the case of a participant with a physical disability. Contribution: This study contributed by framing cognitive surrender as a risk in geometry learning, by positioning professional development as the decisive mediating variable between AI perceptions and classroom practice, and by foregrounding AI as a tool of professional equity for educators with disabilities. These findings contribute to the current research and developments in mathematics education at both the national and international levels by addressing the improvement of mathematics teaching and learning in the South African Senior Phase.

items.title: Sensory Comfort Across Multisensory XR Prototypes for Autistic Adults
items.abstract: Multisensory XR may support autistic adults, yet sensory-friendly design often prioritizes less input. We conducted a mixed-methods, counterbalanced within-subjects study with 20 Chinese autistic adults evaluating five complete XR configurations presenting identical science content: text (L1), text with images (L2), click-triggered spatial audio (L3), gradual light and audio (L4), and L4 plus vibrotactile and thermal cues (L5). The measure combined comfort (Q1), absence of sensory discomfort (Q2), and liking (Q3). Evaluations differed (Friedman χ 2 (4) = 46.39, p <.001, Kendall’s W =.58), and a Q1–Q2 analysis retained the omnibus difference. L3 was lowest ( M = 2.97/5; tied lowest for 16/20). L5 was highest descriptively ( M = 4.43/5), but corrected comparisons did not distinguish it from L1 or L4, and ceiling compression constrained superiority claims. Participants valued clarity, self-pacing, gradual transitions, exit options, and coordinated cues, while disliking abruptness, simultaneous demands, and insufficient warning. These configuration-level findings identify participant-described dimensions for controlled studies.

items.title: Serendipity in recommender systems: a systematic review of definitions, methods, evaluation, and ethics in the era of generative AI
items.abstract: Serendipity, the discovery of unexpected yet valuable items, has become an important objective for recommender systems (RS) aiming to reduce filter bubbles and support long-term user satisfaction. Although accuracy-driven models predict known preferences effectively, they can restrict exploration and reinforce narrow consumption patterns. Despite increasing attention to serendipity as a beyond-accuracy objective, the field remains fragmented because definitions, evaluation protocols, and ethical considerations are not consistently aligned. This systematic review examines serendipity in RS from 2020 to 2025, covering 147 studies and 98 algorithmic contributions. We synthesize diverse definitions into a unified conceptual framework centred on relevance, novelty, and unexpectedness. We also present a methodological taxonomy that traces the field’s evolution from heuristic and traditional approaches to deep learning, knowledge graph, generative, and LLM-based methods. Reported results show that recent LLM-based approaches can achieve strong performance on serendipity-oriented tasks, with $$\:NDC{G}_{seren}$$ scores of up to 0.398. We further review evaluation practices and highlight the gap between computational proxies and subjective user experience. Through quantitative ethical analysis, we show that 74.1% of studies acknowledge ethical concerns, but only 6.8% include dedicated ethics sections, 19.7% operationalize ethical metrics, and 5.4% address content safety. By integrating conceptual, methodological, evaluative, and ethical perspectives, this review provides guidance for developing serendipity-oriented RS that balance relevance with beneficial discovery.

items.title: Service awareness and social influence in the intention to use robo advisors among generation Z adults in India
items.abstract: Little is known about how young prospective users of robo-advisors form their views of them. This study examines how service awareness and social influence relate to perceived ease of use (PEOU), perceived usefulness (PU) and the intention to use robo-advisors among Generation Z adults in India. Responses from 246 respondents aged 18–28 years, collected online through business-school networks in February 2024, were analysed with partial least squares structural equation modelling (PLS-SEM) and confirmatory factor analysis. Service awareness was associated with PEOU (β = 0.387) but not with PU beyond PEOU (β = 0.056, 95% CI [− 0.035, 0.155]). Social influence was associated with both PEOU (β = 0.358) and PU (β = 0.276) and, in an exploratory extended model, directly with intention (β = 0.322). PEOU was associated with intention in every specification. The association between PU and intention was not robust: it was significant in the hypothesised PLS-SEM model (β = 0.291) but not in the covariance-based estimate of that model or, in the exploratory extended model, after the direct path from social influence was added (β = 0.118, 95% CI [− 0.099, 0.327]). PEOU and PU were distinct but closely related (latent correlation 0.883, 95% CI [0.806, 0.943]). Method-factor models did not reach admissible solutions, so method variance could not be quantified. The design is cross-sectional and the sample is a convenience sample, so the estimates are associations for young adults reached through business-school networks, not for rural, non-student or older investors. Trust in algorithms was not measured.

items.title: Shaping Ideas through Questions: Framing Ethical Generative AI Use in Education
items.abstract: The rapid diffusion of generative artificial intelligence (GAI) across teaching, learning, and research demands institutional approaches that are ethical, transparent, and scalable. This study posed the questions: what guiding questions should shape a scalable framework for the ethical use of GAI in educational institutions? Drawing on preliminary results from an ongoing exploratory survey organized around seven categories of GAI engagement, namely: GAI-Powered, GAI-Generated, GAI-Modified, GAI-Revised, GAI-Assembled, GAI-Summarized, and GAI-Rewritten. Respondents consistently emphasized need for human validation, transparency, and attribution as non-negotiable. These findings aligned with international standards and professional guidance (ALA, ACRL and UNESCO etcetera) relevant to higher education and librarianship. The preliminary data from this pilot study included responses from eight participants including students, faculty, and staff across targeted population (education). Based on the results, the guiding questions enabled the proposed framework to address pedagogical, documentation, equity & privacy concerns surrounding ethical use of generative artificial intelligence in educational.

items.title: Shared characterizations of challenging demands and job resources across O*NET element classifications
items.abstract: Purpose Investigations of job characteristics often include an a priori classification of these job elements as either resources or demands. The purpose of this paper was to examine variability in appraisals of job characteristics with respect to perception as resource and/or demand, differential association with positive and negative outcomes and the potential buffering effect of resources on the relationships between demands and negative work outcomes. Design/methodology/approach A sample of 568 working respondents recruited from Prolific completed an online survey. They were asked to think only about their primary job and each administered survey branched content dependent on whether their job could be described as consisting of the different Occupational Information Network (O*NET) job characteristics. Workers also rated the level of resource, challenging demand and hindering demand for each relevant job characteristic. Findings Results support the assertion that job characteristics are not uniquely categorized as a resource or demand, but rather, what is viewed as challenging is also commonly interpreted as resourceful. Furthermore, greater experienced resources moderate the challenge–engagement relationship as well as the hindrance-stress and hindrance–burnout relationships. Originality/value The authors polled a diverse collection of job types across industries who responded to a broad set of characteristics derived from O*NET specifications. They additionally explored characteristics at two levels of aggregation (retaining O*NET category groupings), which again expands their collective knowledge of how employees experience resources, challenges and hindrances within different work domains, as well as the consequences of these experiences.

items.title: Small Clinical Change, Big AI Decision? Metamorphic Testing of Large Language Models in Dental Clinical Decision-Making
items.abstract: Large language model (LLM) chatbots are increasingly consulted for dental decisions, but case-by-case accuracy does not show whether their advice changes when, and only when, a clinically decisive fact changes. Metamorphic testing checks whether answers to two nearly identical cases relate as clinical rules require, without defining a single correct answer for each case. We applied it to oral and maxillofacial surgery and emergency dental decision-making. Thirty guideline-anchored relations were locked before querying, and 60 synthetic case pairs differing in one variable were submitted with a structured prompt to the ChatGPT (GPT-6 Astra) and Gemini (Gemini 3.8) web interfaces. Two blinded specialists scored each pair, with blinded adjudication of disagreements. In the main analysis (58 pairs; two defective vignettes withdrawn), relations were violated in 0 ChatGPT and 8 Gemini pairs (13.8%; p = 0.016, accounting for clustering within relations); with all 60 pairs, 1 vs. 8 (p = 0.063). Gemini violations clustered at numerical thresholds, escalation red flags and a sex-label invariance relation, and 13 of 116 Gemini responses, but no ChatGPT response, contained a safety violation. Chatbots that appear competent case by case can fail at clinically decisive thresholds; metamorphic testing offers a reproducible audit before clinical use.

items.title: Smart City Informatics and Urban Food Environments: A Critical Review of Approaches to Mitigating Commercial Determinants of Poor Nutrition
items.abstract: Poor diet is among the leading modifiable causes of non-communicable disease, and the urban food environment through which commercial actors supply, price, place and promote food is increasingly recognised as a principal pathway linking commercial practices to population nutrition. At the same time, cities are adopting smart city informatics, the integrated use of geospatial, sensor, mobility, transaction, platform and artificial intelligence data to monitor and govern urban systems. Whether these informatics can help mitigate the commercial determinants of poor nutrition, rather than simply describing or even amplifying them, has not been critically examined. This critical narrative review appraises peer-reviewed and institutional literature published between January 2010 and September 2026, identified through structured searching of biomedical and multidisciplinary indexes, citation chasing and institutional sources. Evidence was organised around four questions: how informatics conceptualise and measure urban food environments, what such measurement can and cannot reveal about diet and health, which informatics-enabled approaches have been used to regulate commercial practices, and what governance conditions shape their legitimacy and equity. The synthesis indicates that informatics have substantially improved the scale, temporal resolution and spatial specificity of food environment measurement, particularly through mobility traces, street-level imagery, online food delivery platform data and automated detection of marketing. Associations between measured environments and diet nonetheless remain modest and inconsistent, reflecting exposure misclassification, residential self-selection and the dominance of cross-sectional designs. The strongest evidence of benefit comes not from informatics alone but from regulatory interventions, such as advertising restrictions, planning controls and fiscal measures, whose evaluation was made possible by commercial purchase data and administrative records. Major unresolved problems include dependence on proprietary corporate data, weak validation of machine-learning classifiers, neglect of informal and digital food retail in low- and middle-income countries, and the risk that smart city partnerships reproduce the commercial influence they are intended to counter. Informatics are therefore best understood as enabling infrastructure for accountability and policy evaluation rather than as interventions in their own right. Public data stewardship, transparent validation standards and quasi-experimental evaluation of platform-level regulation are identified as priorities for research and practice.

items.title: Smart Plant Disease Detection System using Deep Learning with Integration of Organic Solutions: A Systematic Review
items.abstract: Detection of plant diseases properly and at the right time is one way of securing the food production process, saving costs and applying chemicals in an inappropriate manner. There have been some advancements made in the area of Deep Learning (DL) that have improved the process of automated diagnosis of plant disease. But most of these systems do not take into consideration the treatment methods that are sustainable. This systematic review examines the present status of Smart Plant Disease Detection Systems (SPDDS) through the application of deep learning techniques along with the adoption of organic solutions in disease detection and management process. For this purpose, a robust review methodology has been used including 102 articles that have been published from 2015 to 2025, focusing on CNNs, Optimization Techniques (GA/PSO) and IoT & Mobile System. Organic treatments for plant diseases have been examined as well in relation to its integration with artificial intelligence technology in diagnosis. In this study, different models have been compared on the basis of accuracy, F1 score, scalability, sustainability of treatment and real-time processing capability.

items.title: Smart Street Light Energy Optimization System Using Artificial Intelligence and Computer Vision
items.abstract: Street lighting accounts for a significant share of municipal electricity consumption, and most installations still operate at full brightness from dusk to dawn regardless of road activity. This paper presents a smart street light system that adjusts lamp intensity according to real-time road activity. Video frames from a roadside camera are processed by a lightweight deep-learning object detector to recognize pedestrians and vehicles; a tracking module assigns persistent identities and estimates movement direction; and a rule-based controller converts the detected activity into a pulse-widthmodulation (PWM) dimming command for an LED driver. When the road is empty, the lamp holds a low baseline level that satisfies minimum safety requirements, and it ramps up when a pedestrian or vehicle is detected in, or approaching, its zone. Two candidate designs were compared, and a detector-plus-tracker pipeline was selected for its balance of accuracy and real-time performance on edge hardware. The selected design reaches 92.6 percent precision and 89.4 percent recall with 34.2 ms inference latency, and the estimated energy saving over constant-output lighting ranges from 34.5 to 65.6 percent depending on traffic density. The work shows that vision-driven adaptive lighting can reduce energy use while preserving road safety and provides a scalable basis for smart-city lighting.

items.title: SMART-Glasses: Low-Power Smoking Monitoring via Acoustic Sensing on Eyewear
items.abstract: The global tobacco epidemic affects the well-being, health, and development of millions of people. While recent advances have greatly improved smoking behaviors monitoring, there remains a lack of widely acceptable, low-power, unobtrusive smoking behaviors monitoring way in real-world scenarios. In this paper, we present SMART ( S moking M onitoring with A coustic Sensing and Sequence R ecognition T echnology)-Glasses, a low-power and minimally obtrusive system that leverages both active and passive acoustic modalities on smart glasses to monitor smoking behavior or recognize the action of lighting a cigarette which enables timely detection, adapting to different user needs. SMART-Glasses innovatively utilizes two speakers and one microphone mounted on the lower rim of the eyeglass frame to emit ultrasonic signals and capture the resulting echoes and passive sounds, thereby extracting features related to smoking behaviors. Furthermore, we introduce a gated sensing enhancement model that amplifies smoking-related features across various noisy conditions. Finally, a smoking action sequence recognition model captures temporal dependencies, allowing the system to distinguish smoking behavior sequences from irrelevant actions. SMART-Glasses is designed for ordinary users who wish to quit smoking and is intended for use in naturalistic environments such as homes, offices, and outdoor areas. Evaluation in both lab and semi-wild settings demonstrates high performance in recognizing lighting and smoking behaviors, showing strong potential for real-world deployment.

items.title: SonicHaptics: Broadband Texture Rendering on Smartphones via Built-in Speaker Airborne Vibration
items.abstract: Haptic feedback on smartphones relies predominantly on Linear Resonant Actuators (LRAs), which operate efficiently only near their resonant frequency and cannot reproduce the broadband vibrations (100–1,000 Hz) required for realistic texture rendering. We present SonicHaptics, a method that repurposes the built-in speaker of a commodity smartphone as a haptic actuator, transmitting airborne vibrations through a fingertip contact piece to render surface textures without additional hardware. The system incorporates a dynamic frequency correction mechanism that tracks finger sliding velocity in real time, enabling texture presentation synchronized with natural exploratory movements. A technical evaluation across four smartphones (iPhone 13, iPhone 15 Pro Max, Pixel 5, and Galaxy S24 Ultra) demonstrates that built-in speakers consistently provide broadband vibration output spanning 100–1,000 Hz, whereas vibration actuators are confined to narrow-band operation. A user study ( N = 30) comparing speaker-based rendering against vibration-actuator-based rendering using three materials with distinct frequency-band characteristics (0–100 Hz, 100–300 Hz, and 300–1,000 Hz) shows that the speaker-based method yields significantly higher realism ratings across all tested bands on the evaluated device, with the largest improvements for mid- and high-frequency textures. Our results establish that repurposing smartphone speakers for haptic rendering is a viable, hardware-free approach to broadband texture presentation on commodity mobile devices.

items.title: SpeakAR: Mitigating Speaking Anxiety via Holographic AR Displays
items.abstract: Speaking anxiety is common and can be influenced by visual cues such as gaze and body language. While many coping strategies focus on preparation ( before speaking) or reflection ( after speaking), our work investigates real-time support delivered in the moment ( during speaking). We present SpeakAR, a real-time intervention that uses head-worn holographic augmented reality (AR) to reshape how speakers view their listeners. SpeakAR introduces two strategies: Audience-Augmentation (AA), which adds virtual elements while preserving audience visibility, and Audience-Occlusion (AO), which reduces access to evaluative audience cues. In an exploratory within-subjects study with 18 participants, we measured speaking anxiety through self-reported distress and acoustic speech features (e.g., jitter, pause rate), and evaluated speech performance through self- and observer-rated assessments. While AA produced mixed effects, AO showed lower anxiety measures and higher observer-rated performance than baseline. These findings highlight AR’s potential to provide support during in-person speaking while revealing trade-offs between anxiety reduction and access to social feedback.

items.title: Sprachmodelle und Kompetenzverschiebungen in der öffentlichen Verwaltung
items.abstract: The rapid adoption of Large Language Models (LLMs) confronts document-intensive public administration with structural changes that impact cognitive work processes and place new demands on staff. This exploratory, qualitative study examines the effects of this technological deployment on the competence profiles of employees in Swiss cantonal and municipal administrations. Based on eight semi-structured expert interviews with HR and digitalization executives, the study draws a nuanced picture of de-skilling, up-skilling, and re-skilling processes. While the automation of routine tasks jeopardizes traditional entry-level positions (de-skilling) and threatens to erode domain knowledge – which is becoming increasingly vital for evaluation and accountability over the longer term – LLMs bring about a perceived increase in autonomy and self-efficacy at the individual level (up-skilling). Contrary to the hypothesis of «metacognitive laziness» frequently postulated in the literature, the dissonance between algorithmic probabilism and the rule-of-law zero-tolerance policy for errors demands an elevation of higher-order thinking skills (re-skilling). The core human contribution shifts from pure text generation toward higher-order thinking skills, requiring verification and accountability skills within human-in-the-loop frameworks. Institutionally, a paradoxical, technology-induced workload inflation is also evident: technological time savings in text production are neutralized by a rising volume of longer, AI-generated external inquiries as well as higher qualitative demands, meaning that the anticipated reduction in workload for staff fails to materialize. The article concludes with strategic recommendations for the proactive and legally compliant management of this socio-technical transformation process.

items.title: Startup sustainability forecasting through natural language processing of business plans
items.abstract: Recent surveys show that only 1 in 400 startups secure funding and achieve post-fund sustainability. Startup assessment is becoming increasingly complicated due to the evolving entrepreneurial landscape, which is affected by too many factors, compelling venture capital firms to harness state-of-the-art Artificial Intelligence (AI). Natural Language Processing (NLP) offers a promising approach for startup assessment, by analyzing documents that summarize key factors of long-term success. Although startup sustainability research is active, modern NLP for assessing business plans has received limited attention. Specifically, the majority of previous works consider only short text descriptions of startups instead of complete business plans, and do not offer adaptability to the varying investment criteria of different investors. In this paper, we propose ForeStart, a startup sustainability forecasting system powered by a transformer-based language model that offers seamless adaptability to the particular needs of users. The proposed system can analyze business plans of unlimited length, including also startup-related content such as pitch deck presentations and company websites. ForeStart is based on a hierarchical Distilled Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers–Bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory (DistilBERT–BiLSTM) architecture trained using both unsupervised domain adaptation and supervised learning, effectively leveraging both unlabeled and labeled business plans. In addition, the proposed system addresses issues arising from privacy concerns and low-resource settings of the startup environment. Our experiments on actual business plans achieve 79% $$F_{1}$$ score in forecasting startup sustainability, even with a limited number of labeled business plans as training data. As an assisting screening tool for analysts, ForeStart can significantly reduce the time required for startup assessments, providing value to Venture Capital (VC) organizations. Moreover, startup founders can also use ForeStart for self-assessment.

items.title: Structural Equation Modelling of ChatGPT Adoption: Testing a Modified UTAUT Model with Moderating Variables
items.abstract: Despite the increasing interest in AI technologies in education, there is a gap in understanding the factors influencing the adoption of ChatGPT among Nigerian higher education students. Research has not comprehensively explored these factors in the Nigerian context, leaving a significant gap in understanding technology adoption in this setting. This study addressed this gap by investigating the predictors of students' behavioural intentions and actual usage behaviour regarding ChatGPT using the UTAUT2 framework. A cross-sectional correlational research design was used in this study. A sample of 8,496 higher education students from diverse institutions in Nigeria participated in the study. The data were collected using the Higher Education Students’ ChatGPT Utilisation Questionnaire (HESCUQ). The findings reveal several significant predictors of students' behavioural intentions and actual usage of the ChatGPT. Performance expectancy, social influence, hedonic motivation, and habit emerged as significant positive predictors of behavioural intention, while effort expectancy and facilitating conditions were significant negative predictors. For ChatGPT use behaviour, facilitating conditions, hedonic motivation, habit, and behavioural intention were significant positive predictors, whereas performance expectancy and social influence were significant negative predictors. items.abstract: How do Library and Information Science (LIS) educators now teach and adapt assessment practices to mitigate the impact of generative AI (GenAI) and support student learning? The emergence of GenAI necessitates critical questions on the assessment strategies and pedagogical practices of LIS educators. Desai (2025) argues that a major challenge of educators in the age of GenAI is how to conduct effective assessments to achieve learning outcomes. This challenge is further compounded by students’ increasing dependence on GenAI technologies for writing and receiving feedback comparable to human tutors (Hamamra et al., 2024). While other disciplines are already developing mechanisms for effective assessments to mitigate the impact of GenAI tools on students (Agbo et al., 2024; Lodge et al., 2023), this intentional strategy by other disciplines seems not to have been given sufficient consideration by Library and Information Science educators around the world, signaling a need for more formal conversations.

items.title: Student Concerns and Perceived Negative Cognitive Effects of AI Tool Use in Academic Settings: A Text Mining Analysis
items.abstract: The growing use of artificial intelligence (AI) tools in academic work has raised concerns about students’ dependence on these tools and possible changes in their learning behaviors. This study examined perceived negative cognitive and behavioral changes reported by 197 college students in relation to their regular academic use of AI tools. Their open-ended responses were analyzed using word-frequency analysis, Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA), Non-negative Matrix Factorization (NMF), and TextBlob sentiment analysis. Topic solutions from two to ten topics were compared based on coherence, consistency across repeated LDA runs, interpretability, and agreement between LDA and NMF. Two topics were retained: behavioral disengagement and AI dependency, and reduced independent cognitive and academic engagement. LDA assigned 130 participants (66%) to the first topic and 67 (34%) to the second, while NMF assigned 124 (62.9%) and 73 (37.1%), respectively. The two models assigned 177 participants (89.8%) to corresponding topics, with κ = .779. The mean TextBlob sentiment score was .090 (SD = .169). TextBlob scores did not differ significantly by sex, U = 4055, p = .081, and showed a small positive relationship with response length, rₛ = .266, p < .001. The findings show that students commonly described dependence, reduced effort, and concerns about independent thinking.

items.title: Student option uptake in a UDL-informed course
items.abstract: Universal access to education and increasing learner variability in Japanese higher education have expanded interest in flexible course design. Grounded in universal design for learning (UDL) and conducted within an action research framework, this practice-focused inquiry examined students’ use of learning-resource options, including Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI), their participation-mode selection in a HyFlex format, and their evaluations of a Japanese junior college course. Students could choose among multiple learning options, including HyFlex participation modes (face-to-face or online) and GenAI use for assignments. Of the 39 students enrolled in the 15-week course, 34 (19 males, 15 females) consented to participate in the study. Data included questionnaire responses (including open-ended items), attendance records, course grades, and institutional course evaluations. The findings revealed that students relied heavily on peers and search engines. Teacher help-seeking increased later in the course as task demands changed. Some students who reported using GenAI described verifying its outputs through search engines. No significant difference was observed between face-to-face and online participation counts, and the number of online attendances did not significantly predict course grades. Most students rated the course positively, and some particularly appreciated the flexibility of the HyFlex format and the teachers’ support and instruction. Overall, this study documents how students selected, used, and evaluated UDL-informed options in one instructional context, derives practice-focused implications for refining technology-enabled course options (e.g., GenAI and HyFlex delivery) and related instructional scaffolds, and suggests that UDL can serve as a lens for interpreting learner variability in course refinement.

items.title: Student Perceptions Toward Research-Based Instructional Strategy in the Era of Large Language Models (LLMs)
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are garnering increasing attention and sparking debate within the educational community among scientific scholars and research-based projects. However, a few studies have addressed the adoption of LLMs in research work, including perceptions, capabilities, and concerns. The current study conducted a survey across one thousand participants from the academic community to assess the adoption capabilities of enhancing, rather than diminishing, the development of students’ research skills. The results revealed a positive perception of the adaptive skillsets associated with LLMs’ adoption, as well as a positive impact on motivation and engagement in the learning process. However, the participants exhibited critical concerns about developing critical thinking skills, language proficiency, and research integrity and authenticity. There was no significant difference in the positive impact of LLM adoption perceptions across demographic groups; however, a significant difference was observed in the perception of research skills development among level of study groups and academic degree groups. Participants also ranked critical thinking and evaluation capability as main measurement criteria in the context of LLM adoption, followed by depth of learning and creativity development.

items.title: Students experiences of using artificial intelligence to learn research methodology: an experiential qualitative study
items.abstract: The rapid integration of generative artificial intelligence (AI) into higher education has transformed the way students learn research methodology, particularly the process of developing research proposals. Although AI-powered tools have become increasingly accessible, limited evidence exists regarding how students experience their use in learning research methods and proposal writing. This study explored the lived experiences of Medical Library and Information Science students using AI tools to learn research methodology and develop research proposals. A qualitative design was adopted to explore students' experiences. Fourteen Medical Library and Information Science students with experience using both general-purpose and domain-specific AI tools for learning research methodology and proposal writing participated and completed Experience Registration Form. Data were analyzed using thematic analysis, with particular attention to students' experiences across key stages of proposal development, including topic selection, problem formulation, literature review and final proposal writing. Five overarching themes emerged: (1) AI as a supportive but potentially dependency forming research companion; (2) Negotiating educational value when selecting AI tools; (3) AI supported learning across the research process; (4) Negotiating the benefits and risks of AI use; (5) Perceived conditions underlying satisfaction with AI assisted learning. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that AI reshaped students' approaches to learning research methodology while simultaneously creating new pedagogical and ethical challenges. Students experienced AI as a cognitive mediator that both facilitated learning research methodology and introduced epistemological and ethical tensions. These findings underscore the importance of integrating critical AI literacy into research methodology education and developing clear institutional guidelines for the responsible use of AI in proposal writing and research training.

items.title: Subjective and Objective QoE Assessment for Real-Time Streaming Interactive Digital Human
items.abstract: Web3 technologies enable novel forms of real-time digital human streaming media by supporting both high-fidelity transmission and interactive user engagement. However, Real-Time Streaming Interactive Digital Humans (RTSIDHs) remain vulnerable to network instability, resulting in buffering, latency, visual degradation, and audio–video desynchronization that substantially impair user Quality of Experience (QoE). To effectively perceive these distortions, we present RDHQA, the first large-scale RTSIDH Quality Assessment dataset. RDHQA comprises 134 representative interaction scenarios with 8 digital human avatars as high-quality references, along with 1,340 distorted samples generated by simulating 5 common streaming degradations. Based on extensive subjective evaluations, we further propose SAV-PF, an audio–visual quality assessment method built on the human foundation model Sapiens and informed by cognitive principles such as the primacy effect and forgetting curve. Experimental results demonstrate that SAV-PF achieves superior performance over existing objective QoE assessment approaches, providing a more accurate prediction of user experience. This work is open sourced at https://github.com/zyj-2000/RDHQA under the CC BY-NC 4.0 licence.

items.title: Survey of the impacts of generative artificial intelligence on critical thinking development in education
items.abstract: Generative AI (GenAI) has been adopted across education faster than its effects on learning have been examined. Critical thinking is among the competencies most consistently demanded of graduates, and whether GenAI use strengthens or weakens it remains unsettled. This review examines how critical thinking is conceptualized and assessed in GenAI-mediated education, what impact GenAI has on students’ critical thinking, and how educators can integrate these tools to support its development. We searched Google Scholar, Semantic Scholar, PubMed, IEEE Xplore, arXiv, and the ACM Digital Library for records on GenAI and education published through June 2026, with no date limit on the conceptual and assessment literature for critical thinking.​ Supplementary background and pedagogical sources also included institutional reports, assessment resources, books, and educational websites. Records were screened in three stages by title, by abstract and conclusion, and by full text, yielding 66 studies for synthesis. GenAI has no uniform effect on critical thinking. Unstructured use is associated with reduced critical thinking enaction, cognitive offloading, and weakened metacognitive monitoring, while use that requires students to interrogate model output is associated with gains, most consistently in analysis and evaluation. The same models produce both outcomes, indicating that the determining variable is the demand the task places on the student. The configurations that produce gains each make reasoning a condition of task progress. Assessment has not kept pace, since instruments that score the submitted artefact cannot separate student reasoning from model contribution. We propose an 18-item self-report instrument that relocates measurement to the process of engaging with AI across all six dimensions of critical thinking. Whether GenAI strengthens or substitutes for student reasoning depends on task and assessment design rather than on the tools themselves.

items.title: Suture stem cells and AI-enabled multi-omics in craniosynostosis: from niche biology to regenerative medicine
items.abstract: Craniosynostosis, the premature fusion of cranial sutures, affects approximately 1 in 2,100–2,500 live births and remains exclusively treated by surgery, which carries risks of resynostosis, secondary intracranial hypertension, and neurodevelopmental sequelae. Over the past decade, the cranial suture has been redefined from a passive fibrous joint into a dynamic stem cell niche: mesenchymal stem and progenitor populations marked by Gli1, Axin2, and Prrx1 reside within the suture mesenchyme, sustain calvarial bone homeostasis, and are depleted or dysregulated in craniosynostosis. In parallel, single-cell RNA sequencing, spatial transcriptomics, and single-nucleus epigenomics have produced the first high-resolution atlases of suture development in mouse and human, while machine learning and deep learning methods increasingly shape diagnosis, phenotyping, and data integration. This review synthesizes these converging lines of evidence for a pediatric neurosurgery and regenerative medicine audience. We first describe the cellular and molecular architecture of the suture stem cell niche and its disruption in syndromic and nonsyndromic craniosynostosis. We then review how multi-omics technologies—single-cell transcriptomics, spatial profiling, and chromatin accessibility mapping—are resolving suture cell states, developmental trajectories, and niche interactions, and how artificial intelligence (AI) methods, from variational autoencoders and trajectory inference to gene regulatory network and cell–cell communication models, convert these data into mechanistic hypotheses. We next examine translational progress, including stem cell-based suture regeneration, biomaterial niche engineering, and patient-derived iPSC disease models, and discuss how AI-assisted biomarker discovery, potency prediction, and quality control could support future cell-based interventions. Finally, we outline outstanding challenges—model interpretability, cross-species and cross-dataset transferability, data standards, and the experimental validation of AI-derived predictions—that must be addressed to move toward reliable regenerative strategies for craniosynostosis.

items.title: Synergising Lean construction and artificial intelligence: a conceptual framework
items.abstract: Purpose The integration of artificial intelligence with Lean construction has been shown to promote added value and drive growth in the built environment. However, understanding of their interaction across multiple levels of abstraction remains limited, especially beyond technical optimisation. This article systematically reviews the interaction between AI and Lean construction to identify current interactions, major applications and research gaps. Design/methodology/approach Following the PRISMA protocol, 63 peer-reviewed studies were identified and analysed qualitatively. AI techniques were mapped against Lean construction principles, waste categories and Lean methods to enable a multi-level comparative synthesis. Findings The results show a growing interest over the past four years, with a focus on AI techniques such as machine learning, optimisation and computer vision used to enhance workflow and to reduce cycle times, particularly within the Last Planner System. Nonetheless, principles centred on value creation, collaboration and partner development remain largely underexplored. Similarly, a co-adaptive relationship was observed to be emerging, in which AI improves Lean's technical efficiency while Lean principles guide AI's development towards ethical and value-driven outcomes. Research limitations/implications The findings offer a foundation for advancing Lean Construction 4.0 through socio-technical integration and human-centred innovation. Practitioners can start by applying mature AI techniques to improve measurable Lean outcomes such as workflow reliability, constraint prediction, visual management and waste reduction, then extend GenAI and NLP tools to collaboration, requirement capture, knowledge reuse and cross-project learning. Originality/value The study proposes a dual-focus model that separates AI's current role as a technical enabler from its future potential as a holistic partner.

items.title: SYNTHID: AI-Based Synthetic Identity and Document Forgery Detection System
items.abstract: SYNTHID is an AI-based synthetic identity and document forgery screening system designed to analyze uploaded identity documents and identify potential signs of visual manipulation or forgery. The system uses artificial intelligence and image analysis techniques to assess document images and generate a tampering-likelihood result. This research presents the design, development, and implementation of SYNTHID, including its web-based interface, image processing workflow, AI-powered forgery screening mechanism, and result visualization. The system aims to assist users in preliminary document authenticity screening by highlighting potential visual irregularities in uploaded documents. SYNTHID is intended as an assistive screening tool and does not independently verify the official validity or issuance of identity documents.

items.title: System of agentic AI for the discovery of metal–organic frameworks
items.abstract: Generative models and machine learning promise accelerated material discovery in metal–organic frameworks (MOFs) for CO 2 capture and water harvesting, but face substantial challenges in navigating vast chemical spaces while ensuring synthesizability. Here we present MOFGen, a system of agentic artificial intelligence (AI) comprising interconnected agents: a large language model that proposes MOF compositions, a diffusion model that generates crystal structures, quantum mechanical agents that optimize and filter candidates, and synthetic-feasibility agents guided by expert rules and machine learning. Trained on a broad set of experimentally reported MOFs and computational databases, MOFGen generated hundreds of thousands of MOF structures and synthesizable organic linkers. The uniqueness of our approach lies in its ability to generate large MOF structures with atomic precision, beyond the scale of conventional generative models limited to tens of atoms. This approach was validated through high-throughput experiments and the successful synthesis of four ‘AI-dreamt’ MOFs.

items.title: TactPrint: A Design Framework for Locally Vibrating Haptic Displays by Optimized Lattice Structures
items.abstract: We introduce TactPrint, a structural design framework for spatial haptic displays that render strong vibrations only in specific regions of an input object. TactPrint replaces a target region of the input object with a simple cubic lattice with sinusoidal-shaped struts and performs parametric optimization to localize vibration at a user-specified frequency. The optimization process uses modal analysis to identify resonance modes characterized by high local vibration amplitudes and iteratively updates shape parameters to align the resonance frequency with the target frequency. Users can then directly fabricate the optimized structure using a 3D printer and render the localized vibration with an attached actuator. This framework enables the design of haptic devices with spatially localized vibration without considering physical constraints or structural dynamics. In this paper, we investigate the error between simulation and measurement on fabricated objects, the designable frequency range, and the usability of the workflow. Finally, we demonstrate several application examples.

items.title: Taking a Pulse on How Generative AI is Reshaping the Software Engineering Research Landscape
items.abstract: Context: Software engineering (SE) researchers increasingly study Generative AI (GenAI) while also incorporating it into their own research practices. Despite rapid adoption, there is limited empirical evidence on how GenAI is used in SE research and its implications for research practices and governance. Aims: We conduct a large-scale survey of 456 SE researchers publishing in top venues (2023–2025). Method: Using quantitative and qualitative analyses, we examine who uses GenAI and why, where it is used across research activities, and how researchers perceive its benefits, opportunities, challenges, risks, and governance. Results: GenAI use is widespread, with many researchers reporting pressure to adopt and align their work with it. Usage is concentrated in writing, data processing, and analysis, while goal formulation and study design remain largely human-driven. Although productivity gains are widely perceived, concerns about trust, correctness, and regulatory uncertainty persist. Researchers highlight risks such as inaccuracies and bias, emphasize mitigation through human oversight and verification, and call for clearer governance, including guidance on responsible use and peer review. Conclusion: We provide a fine-grained, SE-specific characterization of GenAI use across research activities, along with taxonomies of GenAI use cases for research and peer review, opportunities, risks, mitigation strategies, and governance needs. These findings establish an empirical baseline for the responsible integration of GenAI into academic practice.

items.title: Talking Manual: An AI-Powered Industrial Maintenance Copilot
items.abstract: Maintenance technicians waste time looking up information in manuals, procedures and asking colleagues about what went wrong whilst attempting to fix a problem. This means those trying to fix the issue have little opportunity to type or interact with a screen due to gloves, dirt on their hands or holding tools. This paper introduces Talking Manual, an AI-based maintenance assistant which allows every industrial machine to have its own persistent knowledge base. Grease Mode is a non-contact gesture and voice-based interface for interacting with this knowledge base. Each equipment manual is processed by a layout aware OCR engine, chunked into 512 tokens and stored in a ChromaDB collection specific to that machine. Diagrams are extracted and converted into text using a Qwen2.5-VL vision language model. A Retrieval Augmented Generation pipeline was developed to answer questions. Dense and keyword search are performed using vector store and keyword search respectively. The results are re-ranked using a BGE re-ranker and responses are generated using Gemini 1.5 Pro. A four state diagnosis checklist (pending, completed, rejected, outdated) is updated by the language model. If a step is rejected in the checklist it changes the diagnosis flow. This is provided by using a stream intercept layer. Grease Mode provides gesture control. This is done using MediaPipe Hands in the Browser. The features are relative to the wrist of the user, and therefore the ONNX classifier can be used. The gestures are debounced so frames are maintained. This means no video is sent out of the device. Voice dictation is used constantly. Audio at 16kHz is sent over a WebSocket to a local GPU. Fast whisper large-v3 is run on the audio using int8_float16 quantization. Testing during development showed that having lossless diagrams, off-loading to background threads and quantizing the speech model to 8 bits was required to ensure accurate and quick responses using only 6Gb of GPU memory. A protocol to evaluate this system is provided using quantifiable metrics. The system has been tested quantitatively. This shows how well the system performs by looking at the accuracy, information retrieval, and gesture recognition. This demonstrates that the system can support users in retrieving industrial maintenance information using voice and gesture.. Index Terms—retrieval augmented generation, industrial maintenance, large language models, guided diagnosis, mixed retrieval, multi-modal retrieval, hand gesture detection, non contact interface, speech recognition, copilot.

items.title: Teachers' instructional practices in neoliberal era: Impact on students' achievement motivation in the classroom
items.abstract: Neoliberalism has re-engineered education into a market-driven, performance-oriented system that prioritizes standardised metrics over a spirit of inquiry. This article explores how this shift undermines teachers’ teaching abilities, highly impacts their self-efficacy and compromises students' achievement motivation. To counteract this rigid framework, the following article argues that educators must cultivate symbiotic classroom relationships and prioritize social-emotional learning. Doing so, it is essential to liberate cognitive engagement and rescue holistic academic outcomes from corporate constraints. While it is necessary to prepare individuals for jobs and realistic challenges, it is also crucial to focus on the achievement motivation of the students keeping in mind the individual differences and tempering their responsiveness to demanding situations. It also highlights the need to take a critical approach towards the academic performance of the students in the academic settings by looking at it from the psychological lens.

items.title: Tecnologias digitais e acessibilidade na 3ª idade: estratégias para adiar o fim do mundo
items.abstract: The population of older adults in [omitted] accounts for approximately 20% of the total population. Part of this group resides in rural communities and has limited digital literacy. In response, the project addressed a demand from the Social Assistance Reference Center (CRAS) to support adults aged 60 and over in accessing digital applications. The project consisted of five workshops involving 160 participants. The methodological approach was inspired by Ailton Krenak’s Ideas to Postpone the End of the World, with activities facilitated by adolescents and culminating in handcrafted artistic products. The workshops were grounded in Mana Bernardes’ idea of Finding people within people and the oral narrative of the Matryoshka. Participants engaged in intergenerational exchanges through smartphone support, with students acting as mediators. The groups then discussed technology in light of Krenak’s work and concluded that ancestral knowledge embodies innovative potential and constitutes a form of technology applicable today. As a final activity, participants customized bags made from recycled textile scraps. The outcomes highlight the value of intergenerational encounters that bring together artificial intelligence and ancestral intelligence as complementary forms of knowledge, fostering digital inclusion and contributing to the broader goal of postponing the end of the world.

items.title: TesselTex: Modulating Tactile Experience of Texture Roughness on Actuated Surfaces Composed of Tessellated Everyday Materials
items.abstract: Many studies in Human–Computer Interaction (HCI) have explored the tactile experience of material textures for its potential in virtual reality and tangible interaction. We introduce TesselTex, an inflatable silicone-based structure, consisting of a tessellated matrix of textured “pixel”s made from two materials with differing roughness. By inflating embedded air chambers, skin contact between different materials on the tessellated surface can be adjusted, thereby modulating users’ tactile perception of textures. We investigated how users perceived fine roughness and surface bumpiness under different pneumatically-controlled “pixel” heights, with TesselTex samples of different “pixel” densities and material compositions, in active (finger) and passive (forearm) stroking interactions. Results showed that pneumatic lifting of the material “pixels” significantly decreased user-perceived roughness in composite samples, an effect not observed in conventional single-material bump arrays. Meanwhile, “pixel” lifting significantly increased perceived surface bumpiness during active finger exploration, but had slight opposite effect under passive forearm stroking. In addition, higher “pixel” density slightly increased the perceived roughness of the surface and modulated bumpiness perception, depending on the interaction mode.

items.title: The “Gowisha” Phenomenon: Vernacular Camouflage and Digital Coping Mechanisms among South African Youth
items.abstract: Digital expression of distress in the Global South often circumvents Western clinical vocabulary through vernacular substitution. This study examines gowishing, a South African idiom for severe distress, across TikTok, Instagram, and X. Drawing on a dataset of 78,538 posts and comments, including a census of 10,366 idiom items and 10,940 items coded by large language model coders, it analyses how users deploy code-switching, slang, and emoji as linguistic camouflage. In the census, 88.9\% of uses convey distress. An English-centric rule treating comic delivery as evidence against distress erased about two-thirds of measured mental-health content in Sotho-Tswana languages, two-fifths in Nguni languages, and a fifth in English, but none in Afrikaans. Camouflage proves bidirectional and shows signs of commercial capture. The study extends Goffman's stigma theory through boyd's context collapse, updated for algorithmic platforms, and puts both in dialogue with Ubuntu-informed communal distress, treating their unresolved tension as its central contribution.

items.abstract: The Artist of Tomorrow: Conductor or Mere Performer? An Interdisciplinary Exploratory Review of Human Creativity, Artificial Intelligence, and Copyright Law This interdisciplinary exploratory review examines the evolving role of human creativity in an era of artificial intelligence, automation, and digital artistic production. Through a historical perspective spanning several centuries, the study explores major technological and artistic transitions, including photography, cinema, sound recording, conceptual art, digital editing, and generative artificial intelligence. Particular attention is given to the distinction between technical execution and human creative intention, examining how artistic originality may emerge through selection, composition, interpretation, and creative direction rather than manual production alone. The review also addresses legal questions surrounding copyright protection, public-domain works, AI-assisted restoration, and human authorship, drawing on French, European, and American legal frameworks. A case study involving the 1925 film The Phantom of the Opera illustrates the complexities of audiovisual restoration, original musical contributions, and derivative creative elements. The HUMAN.zip exploratory framework further examines human–AI collaboration, highlighting methodological limitations, interpretative biases, and opportunities for future comparative research. Central hypothesis: "Automating execution does not necessarily mean automating creation." This publication aims to contribute to interdisciplinary discussions on artistic authorship, technological transformation, intellectual property, and the future relationship between human creativity and artificial intelligence. Keywords: Artificial Intelligence, Human Creativity, Copyright Law, Artistic Originality, Human–AI Collaboration, Digital Art, Cinema History, Public Domain, Generative AI, HUMAN.zip. items.title: The Author and Its Forms in the Digital Age: From Word to ChatGPT
items.abstract: In recent years, both public and academic interest has increasingly turned toward artificial intelligence (AI) and the literature generated by computational language models. This article examines the question of authorship in relation to such models - whether and in what form authorship can be attributed to them. To address this issue, the article first explores the history of electronic writing and the emergence of discourses that, despite originating in the pre-digital era, remain relevant today. Beyond tracing the metamorphosis of the author’s role and the reader’s position, the article focuses on how the dynamics of these relationships are reshaped by AI-driven language models - highlighting both the dangers and opportunities they present for texts, their creators, and their recipients. Finally, the article addresses the challenges that arise when the concepts of originality and authenticity - traditionally associated exclusively with human creativity and consciousness - are applied to our understanding of AI-generated literature.
