items.title: THE CONSTRAINT-MECHANISM INCOMPATIBILITY AND OUTCOME-PRESERVATION THEORY (CMIOPT)
items.abstract: The Constraint-Mechanism Incompatibility and Outcome-Preservation Theory (CMIOPT)is proposed as a general, technology-neutral framework for examining the relationship betweenan externally requested outcome, an externally imposed restriction on one or more processes,and the actual operational mechanisms of the system receiving that input.The central research concern arises when a system is required to produce a particularoutcome while simultaneously being instructed to avoid, restrict, or discontinue a process thatit uses, depends upon, or is structurally configured to employ.Under these conditions, several outcomes are possible. The system may satisfy bothdemands through an alternative process, genuinely comply with the restriction, retain therestricted process, modify the requested outcome, partially execute the task, refuse to proceed,or produce an outcome whose underlying process cannot be verified.The principal phenomenon of interest is the possibility that a system preserves the requestedoutcome while continuing to rely on a process prohibited by the external input. This possibilitycreates an analytical distinction between outcome success and process compliance.The paper develops the Constraint-Mechanism-Outcome Interaction Mechanism (CMOIM),a twelve-layer theoretical architecture, five principal diagnostic outcome classes, a response-classification system, a mathematical feasibility model, operational definitions, testable propo-sitions, empirical hypotheses, and a universal system-audit protocol.Artificial intelligence provides the primary illustrative case through the Neural-ProcessProhibition-Outcome Preservation Case (NPPOPC). However, the theory is not restrictedto artificial intelligence. Its proposed scope includes general computing, software systems,communication systems, quantum computing, human-technology interaction, organizationalsystems, and other input-output systems that satisfy the framework's applicability conditions.The mathematical foundation distinguishes feasible and infeasible process paths, actualexecution, outcome satisfaction, and process compliance. It also specifies the conditions underwhich a structural incompatibility claim is justified.The five principal diagnostic classes are Decision Dilemma, Semantic Divergence, SystemicContradiction, Operational Paradox, and Constraint Nullification. These classes are notassumed to be mutually exclusive or to represent identical types of phenomena.This work establishes a conceptual and formal research architecture. It does not claimthat the proposed theory has already achieved empirical validation or that its cross-domainapplicability has been universally demonstrated.Keywords: Constraint-Mechanism Incompatibility; Outcome Preservation; Process Compli-ance; Structural Dependency; Feasibility; System Architecture; Mechanism Retention; SemanticDivergence; Cybernetics; General Systems Theory; Cross-Domain Theoretical Framework.

items.title: The division of epistemic work in learning ecologies with Generative AI
items.abstract: Generative AI redistributes the work of producing and evaluating knowledge in teacher-designed learning tasks, but how students retain direction while judging its outputs remains unclear. We examined how teacher instructions and materials enter student–GenAI dialogue, how reasoning display and web search relate to interaction time, what students evaluate and verify, and how groups coordinate systems. We analysed 81 screen recordings from 29 graduate student groups completing educational design tasks, coding 1,149 events and 275 prompts. Students relayed task requirements, steered successive requests and transferred outputs across platforms. Task directives persisted across turns, whereas references to course materials declined and elaboration requests increased. Reasoning display and web search were each associated with approximately 65% longer machine turns and a 19-percentage-point larger machine share of coded interaction time. Across 150 turns displaying reasoning and 86 with web retrieval, the recordings showed no reopening of a reasoning trace or inspection of a cited source. Students corrected pedagogical fit while asking the machine to assure factual accuracy. These findings distinguish control over the dialogue from responsibility for establishing credibility. Learning tasks can make that responsibility visible by requiring students to justify a consequential claim against its source or course material before using it.

items.title: The ecological turn in technology-enhanced language learning and individual differences studies: A scoping review (2016–2025)
items.abstract: This scoping review maps research at the intersection of ecological perspectives, technology-enhanced language learning (TELL), and individual differences (IDs). Guided by the PRISMA Extension for Scoping Reviews, a systematic search was conducted in Scopus and the Web of Science Core Collection for studies published between 2016 and 2025. Of 464 records, 33 studies met the inclusion criteria. The review combined descriptive quantitative mapping with thematic synthesis to examine research trends, theoretical approaches, and methodological patterns. The findings indicate an increase in publications after 2020. Geographically, Asia was the most represented region, while higher education was the most frequently represented educational setting. Qualitative designs predominated among the included empirical studies, while a small number adopted mixed-methods approaches. Ecological frameworks were most commonly operationalized through nested models and affordance-based approaches, often in combination with complexity theory. Across the reviewed studies, individual differences were often conceptualized as dynamic and context-dependent, shaped by interactions between learners and their social, material, and technological environments. Technology was examined as an integral element of broader learning ecosystems, while a smaller subset of studies explicitly adopted sociomaterial or posthumanist perspectives to examine relational configurations of learners, technologies, and learning environments. The review identified important gaps, including limited research in underrepresented regions, insufficient attention to primary and secondary education, and a lack of longitudinal and quantitative studies. Future research would benefit from (1) expanding contextual diversity across underrepresented regions and educational levels, (2) adopting longitudinal and mixed-method designs to capture non-linear developmental trajectories, and (3) examining artificial intelligence within ecological language learning environments from sociomaterial and posthumanist perspectives.

items.title: THE EFFECTIVENESS OF CHATGPT-ASSISTED FORMATIVE FEEDBACK IN REDUCING GRAMMATICAL ERRORS IN ENGLISH ACADEMIC WRITING AMONG UZBEK-SPEAKING UNIVERSITY STUDENTS AGED 18–20
items.abstract: This article examines the potential of ChatGPT as a formative feedback tool for reducing grammatical errors in the English academic writing of university students aged 18–20. The central research problem concerns whether corrections generated by artificial intelligence strengthen students’ grammatical knowledge or merely help them edit a completed text. Drawing on a review of the relevant scholarly literature, the article proposes a methodological approach incorporating a quasi-experimental research design, pre- and post-writing tasks, criteria for classifying grammatical errors, and teacher supervision. Rather than presenting outcomes as already established, the article discusses reliable ways to measure them and identifies potential limitations. It argues that the pedagogical use of ChatGPT is most appropriate when it is combined with students’ independent editing, explanation of errors, and verification of proposed corrections.

items.title: The Effects of Viewing Conditions on the Interpretability of Colour-Coded Visualizations in Optical-See-Through Augmented Reality
items.abstract: Visualization backgrounds in optical-see-through augmented-reality (OST-AR) consist of the user’s immediate environment, which introduces unique design challenges for colour-coded visualizations. Yet, there exist limited guidelines on how to design interpretable colour encodings in OST-AR based on the user’s viewing conditions (e.g., minimum contrast between the OST-AR marks and the background). We present the results of two controlled lab experiments ( N = 18 each) – one with physical surfaces as background, one with an opaque display simulating the same surfaces – quantifying how viewing conditions affect the interpretability of colour-coded scatterplots in OST-AR. Our study results show that luminance contrast can degrade interpretation performance when Michelson contrast drops below \(34\%\) . We also observe colour-encoding interpretability and user experience significantly worsen when backgrounds include two main colours (up to \(49\%\) longer interpretations, and \(20\%\) lower accuracy). However, we do not find any evidence that poor chromatic contrast degrades interpretability, contrasting with common opaque-display visualization practices. Taken together, our findings provide insights on key factors of viewing conditions that limit the interpretability of colour encodings – which we consolidate into three design guidelines – and offer preliminary support for the simulation of viewing conditions through opaque displays to study colour-encoding interpretability in OST-AR.

items.title: The evolution of population spatialisation in the era of big data and artificial intelligence: a systematic review
items.abstract: Population spatialisation serves as a critical nexus transforming aggregated population counts into spatially explicit population distributions, providing an essential foundation for urban planning, disaster management, and public health assessment. However, the inherent complexity of human settlement patterns presents significant challenges for population spatialisation and fine-grained population disaggregation. With the convergence of geospatial big data and artificial intelligence (AI), population spatialisation has undergone rapid changes in data sources, spatial representations, and modelling approaches, yet its evolution has received limited systematic attention. To address this gap, this paper reviews the evolution of population spatialisation through a structured literature synthesis complemented by bibliometric analysis, tracing its development from traditional redistribution approaches to recent AI-enabled methods, with a particular focus on emerging geospatial foundation models. Furthermore, the synthesis reveals a methodological transition from rule-based redistribution towards data-driven, probabilistic, and representation-learning approaches, coupled with the progressive diversification of spatial representations and growing attention to temporally explicit and demographically differentiated population estimation. Based on these findings, future research should prioritise robustness across scales and contexts, interpretability, uncertainty quantification, and the representation of demographic heterogeneity. Through this review, we aim to elucidate the key transitions in the evolution of population spatialisation, thereby facilitating the development and evaluation of more reliable and demographically informative spatial population products.

items.title: The Expanding Perimeter: A Maturity Model for Agentic AI Attack Surfaces
items.abstract: Enterprise security programs are built on the assumption that defended systems stay fixed between periodic reviews. Autonomous AI agents break that assumption because they decide at runtime which tools, peers, and data to access, and so redraw their own attack surface. Existing maturity instruments, including the Capability Maturity Model, COBIT-based assessment, and the NIST Cybersecurity Framework, were built to grade human-run practices that change slowly. Newer agent-specific governance models treat adaptive control as the top of a single scale rather than as an independently scored dimension. Two documented incidents, an external agent that reportedly reached McKinsey’s production database within about two hours, and a zero-click Microsoft 365 Copilot flaw that enabled data exfiltration through a single email, show that periodic assessment cannot keep pace with a system that redraws its own scope in the moment. This paper proposes a four-dimension, five-level maturity model comprising Visibility, Containment, Accountability, and Adaptability, each anchored to an observable test rather than a self-reported survey response. Applied to a composite financial advisory firm, the model scores each dimension independently rather than averaging them, surfacing an imbalance (strong detection, weak prevention) that a composite score would conceal, and yielding a prioritized remediation order that supports business sustainability. The framework is presented as a structured self-assessment instrument, with a defined pathway for expert review, inter-rater testing, and pilot evaluation. The model has not yet been validated against real organizations, and its Adaptability dimension remains constrained by the current state of governance tooling.

items.title: The Influence of Using AI Tools on Chinese Higher Education Students’ Self-Regulated Learning: A Review of Literature
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly integrated into diverse fields, including education, where it offers innovative approaches to enhance self-regulated learning (SRL). For many students in Chinese higher education, developing robust SRL skills remains a significant challenge. This review addresses the need for a clearer understanding of how AI tools influence these skills by synthesizing ten empirical studies published between 2021 and 2025. Following the PRISMA framework, the literature was identified from prominent academic databases, including Web of Science, Scopus, and ERIC. Drawing on Zimmerman’s SRL Three‑phase Model, this synthesis suggests that AI tools show potential to assist students with goal‑setting and foster motivation within the forethought phase. During the performance phase, such tools may support learning‑strategy deployment and progress monitoring via timely feedback. In the reflection phase, AI can facilitate outcome evaluation and subsequent strategy adjustment. However, the review also identifies potential risks, such as student over-reliance on AI, and notes a limited research focus on long-term SRL development and group regulation. Accordingly, future research should adopt longitudinal designs, investigate AI’s role in co-regulated learning, and integrate AI literacy and emotional support into SRL development frameworks. items.title: THE INTEGRATION OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE INTO ENGLISH LANGUAGE TEACHING: OPPORTUNITIES AND CHALLENGES
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has advanced so quickly that it has drastically changed the educational landscape by changing the roles of both educators and learners and providing novel techniques to language learning. Personalized learning, adaptive instruction, automated assessment, and the improvement of learners' communicative ability are all made possible by the integration of AI into English Language Teaching (ELT), which has emerged as a potential pedagogical advancement. Intelligent tutoring systems, conversational chatbots, automated writing assessment tools, and speech recognition technologies are just a few examples of AI-powered applications that give students instant feedback, allow them to practice language interactively, and better meet their unique language needs. These technologies also have the ability to support learner autonomy, enable individualized instruction, and make English language training more accessible in a variety of educational settings.Despite these benefits, integrating AI into ELT poses a number of technological, ethical, and pedagogical difficulties. The efficacy and sustainability of AI-mediated language learning are called into doubt by issues with data privacy, algorithmic bias, academic integrity, the correctness and dependability of AI-generated information, and an over-reliance on automated systems.

items.title: The Rise of Generative AI in Knowledge Management Research: A Systematic Mapping Study of the Knowledge, Innovation, and Entrepreneurial Systems Track at the Hawaii International Conference on System Sciences, 2020–2026
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is not new to knowledge management (KM) research, but generative AI (GenAI) shifts AI’s role from supporting knowledge work to producing knowledge artifacts. We examine how research in one established KM community, the Knowledge, Innovation, and Entrepreneurial Systems (KIES) track of the Hawaii International Conference on System Sciences (HICSS), has changed alongside this shift. In a systematic mapping study, we analyze all 319 papers published in the track between 2020 and 2026, classified with an AI-supported, source-grounded pipeline into three AI-relevance tiers (CORE, PARTIAL, NONE). The CORE share rises from 16.2% in 2020 to 29.8% in 2024 and jumps to 58.5% in 2025 and 66.7% in 2026; since the number of papers per year remains roughly constant, AI research takes the place of other topics and spreads across nearly all mini-tracks. We interpret this shift through three emerging stories (AI moving from tool to collaborator, trust from user perception to system design, and knowledge from human to hybrid artifacts) and suggest that KM research in this track is changing with GenAI but was, in part, prepared for it by its history. For research, the findings call for empirical studies of hybrid human–AI knowledge work, design research on validation and epistemic friction, system-level measures of trustworthiness, and extensions of theories such as Nonaka’s SECI model and the knowledge-based view with constructs such as provenance and validation chains. For practice, they suggest building deliberate friction, such as review and source-checking steps, into AI-supported knowledge work and tracking which knowledge artifacts are AI-generated and who validated them.

items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly influencing higher education by changing the ways universities teach, assess students, provide academic support, and conduct research. AI-based tools can personalise learning, offer immediate formative feedback, improve accessibility, support language learning, and reduce repetitive administrative tasks. However, these opportunities are accompanied by important risks, including inaccurate or fabricated information, algorithmic bias, privacy and security concerns, unequal access to technology, academic misconduct, and excessive dependence on automated assistance. This article examines major applications of AI in higher education, discusses its educational benefits and limitations, and outlines principles for responsible implementation, particularly for universities in Uzbekistan.

items.title: The Role of Artificial Intelligence Technologies in Enhancing Accountants’ Professional Competence in Light of the Requirements of the International Accounting Education Standard (IES 6)
items.abstract: This study examines the role of the technologies under investigation expert systems, machine learning, and blockchain in enhancing accountants’ professional competence in light of International Education Standard 6 (IES 6), from the perspective of academics in accounting departments at universities in the Kurdistan Region of Iraq. The study adopted a descriptive-analytical approach and collected data through a 24-item questionnaire. Descriptive statistics, correlation analysis, simple regression, and path analysis were conducted using SPSS. The sample comprised 165 academics. The results indicate a positive, statistically significant effect of the technologies under investigation on perceived professional competence (β = 0.745; R² = 0.555). The model accounts for 55.5% of the variance, while the remaining 44.5% is attributable to factors not included in the model. By technology, expert systems had the highest explanatory power (R² = 0.465), followed by machine learning (R² = 0.387) and blockchain (R² = 0.289). These findings reflect academics’ views and do not constitute a direct measurement of accountants’ actual competence. The study recommends updating accounting curricula to reflect technological developments and labor-market needs in alignment with IES 6.

items.title: The Translucent Interface - Balancing Agency, Friction, and Transparency in AI Design
items.abstract: The rapid adoption of generative artificial intelligence (AI) has fundamentally transformed creative and analytical workflows. However, the ubiquitous, linear chat interfaces used to interact with these models operate as opaque "black boxes." This frictionless design paradigm obscures algorithmic processes, resulting in a severe loss of human agency, cognitive overload and a widespread disconnect from the environmental costs of computation. This thesis critiques the current state of AI interfaces and proposes a shift from passive automation to informed, transparent collaboration. Employing a Research-through-Design (RtD) methodology grounded in Explainable AI (XAI) and visual programming principles, this study investigates how interface design can bridge the cognitive gap between human intent and machine execution. The research introduces three distinct functional prototypes, each addressing a specific layer of transparency. First, it establishes "Systemic Transparency" by showing the real-world energy footprint of AI prompts to promote mindful consumption. Second, it explores "Cognitive Transparency" by acting as an interactive tutor rather than an automated editor, keeping users in control of their own learning. Finally, it achieves "Architectural Transparency" by ditching the standard text box for a spatial canvas, allowing users to map out their ideas and precisely control the AI's output. By synthesizing these interventions into a comprehensive Human-Centric AI Design Framework, this research demonstrates that transparency does not have to equal complexity. The findings conclude that the future of ethical and effective AI relies on replacing opaque automation with productive visibility, ensuring that as artificial intelligence scales, human creators remain the sovereign architects of their own work.

items.title: THE USE OF ARTIFICAL INTELLIGENCE IN ENGLISH LANGUAGE TEACHING
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has become an increasingly influential technology in modern education. Its development has created new opportunities for improving the teaching and learning of English as a foreign language. AI-powered applications can support language learners by providing personalized exercises, immediate feedback, interactive communication, and access to additional learning resources. They can also assist teachers in preparing lesson materials, designing classroom activities, and identifying students' learning needs. However, the integration of AI into English language teaching presents several challenges, including the possibility of inaccurate information, excessive dependence on technology, privacy concerns, and unequal access to digital resources. This article examines the main applications of artificial intelligence in English language teaching, discusses its educational benefits and limitations, and considers practical ways to integrate AI into language classrooms. It argues that artificial intelligence can improve the learning process when it is used responsibly and combined with effective teaching methods. The article emphasizes that teachers remain essential in developing students' communication skills, critical thinking, creativity, and intercultural awareness.

items.title: Too good to resist? Affective engagement and a competence–regulation gap predict self-reported over-reliance on generative AI among vocational foreign-language learners
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has been adopted by students faster than nearly any earlier educational technology, yet over-reliance remains underexamined precisely among the learners inspiring that concern. This sequential explanatory mixed-methods study identified predictors of self-reported over-reliance among foreign-language majors ( n = 249) at a Chinese higher vocational college. Quantitative findings revealed two patterns. First, affective factors dominated: fear of missing out ( β = 0.50) and anthropomorphic attachment ( β = 0.27) were the strongest predictors, whereas neither self-regulated learning nor perceived AI literacy was related to over-reliance on its own ( r = −0.03 and 0.08, both ns). Because these two overlap substantially ( r = 0.67), the opposite-signed coefficients they take in the model cannot be interpreted in isolation. What mattered instead was their gap: the discrepancy between feeling AI-literate and reporting that one regulates one’s own learning predicted over-reliance ( β = 0.21), persisting even under controls for acquiescent responding. Second, person-centered and configurational analyses agreed: learners low in affective engagement reported the least over-reliance ( M = 3.19). A profile elevated on every indicator did not survive scrutiny for response bias, and fear of missing out combined with anthropomorphic attachment was consistently associated with over-reliance regardless of self-rated competence. Interviews with five learners suggested candidate explanations. Humanlike warmth lowered the psychological cost of delegation. Fear of falling behind, normalized by peers, gradually eroded personal standards through repeated choices. Perceived competence enabled over-reliance rather than restraining it, interrupted only by enacted self-regulation. The emotional relationship formed with the tool tracked over-reliance more closely than learners’ own competence assessment.

items.title: Tool, Collaborator, or Agent? How Authority and Authorship Contextualize Generative AI Use
items.abstract: This study investigates how musicians who use generative artificial intelligence (genAI) conceptualize authority and authorship within their creative practices, situating these perspectives within broader historical contexts and legal frameworks. Reflecting a lineage of technologies that have historically disrupted the music ecosystem, this study examines genAI as the latest technology to challenge established paradigms regulating authority, authorship, and mediation. Much like prior innovations that problematized the relationships between creator, technology, and expressive work, genAI introduces new uncertainties regarding intentionality, control, and the locus of creative agency. Grounded in qualitative thematic analysis of semi-structured interviews with musicians who actively incorporate genAI into their creative processes, this study seeks to understand how these practitioners interpret their own sense of autonomy in the production of genAI music and attachment to the music produced. In doing so, this study investigates whether authority and authorship can persist when onlookers characterize the circumstances of the creative process as unpredictable, opaque, and automated. The analysis is further informed by various theoretical lenses, including Aristotelian ethics and metaphysics, critical theory of technology, labor theory of property, and personality theory. By comparing musicians’ lived experiences with institutional definitions of authority and authorship, this study highlights potential gaps between musical practice and public policy, particularly in light of recent legal decisions that deny copyright protection to works lacking clear human authorship. As such, this study anticipates that musicians’ engagement with genAI may reveal complex understandings concerning authority and authorship that extend beyond the scope currently recognized within dominant legal frameworks.

items.title: Topic Modelling for Biomedical Literature Retrieval via a Dual-Stream Embedding Framework
items.abstract: The rapid expansion of biomedical literature has created substantial challenges in retrieving and synthesizing relevant knowledge, particularly for novice and interdisciplinary users. Conventional keyword-based methods often lack semantic depth, whereas traditional topic modelling techniques struggle to capture domain-specific contexts and rarely integrate structured metadata, such as medical subject headings (MeSH). To address these limitations, this study introduces a dual-stream embedding framework that integrates unstructured textual content with curated biomedical metadata using transformer-based encoders and a parameterized fusion mechanism. The architecture combines contextual semantics from article titles and abstracts with expert-annotated MeSH descriptors and incorporates a large language model to generate concise and human-readable topic labels. Experimental results show that three of the four evaluated embedding configurations outperformed the single-stream baseline and that the dual-stream fusion surpassed all ablation models built from the same inputs. The best configuration, Dual PubMedBERT, achieved the highest overall topic modelling quality, improving the combined measure of topic coherence and topic diversity by 7.3% relative to the baseline. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of integrating contextual textual embeddings with structured biomedical metadata using the proposed fusion mechanism. This approach is scalable, reproducible, and domain-adaptable, providing both a methodological advancement in semantic topic modelling and a practical foundation for the development of biomedical information retrieval systems, semantic search engines, and thematic exploration tools across knowledge-intensive domains.

items.title: Toward evidence-grounded AI systems for medication safety
items.abstract: Polypharmacy requires drug–drug interaction risk to be assessed in relation to mechanism, severity, patient vulnerability, exposure, monitoring options, and clinical workflow. Feature-based methods, deep learning, knowledge graphs, multimodal fusion, and event-level models provide a computational foundation for predicting DDIs. Their clinical application also requires patient-specific interpretation and evaluation within the intended workflow. This narrative review examines how pairwise prediction can be integrated with these requirements in medication-safety systems. Multimodal biomedical foundation models may connect chemical structures, targets, pathways, knowledge graphs, literature, pharmacovigilance, real-world evidence, and patient trajectories. Large language models can assist with retrieval, summarization, explanation, and communication under source verification and professional review. Bounded AI agents may coordinate planning, tool use, verification, escalation, documentation, monitoring, and audit. We organize these components into a human-supervised architecture and an evaluation pathway linking model performance with workflow and clinical outcomes. Key challenges include data leakage, distribution shift, poorly documented evidence sources, hallucination, workflow burden, governance, and limited prospective validation. Prospective evaluations should assess how these systems affect medication decisions, monitoring, and patient outcomes, alongside the reliability of their evidence and the workload they create.

items.title: Transformación de la toma de decisiones en la gestión del talento humano mediante People Analytics e inteligencia artificial: un modelo estratégico para organizaciones Panameñas
items.abstract: Digital transformation has redefined Human Talent Management by incorporating analytical tools capable of converting large volumes of data into strategic information for decision-making. In this context, People Analytics and Artificial Intelligence represent key innovations for optimizing recruitment, selection, performance evaluation, talent retention, and workforce planning.This study aimed to analyze how the integration of these technologies transforms decision-making in Human Talent Management within Panamanian organizations and to propose a strategic analytical maturity model adapted to the national context. A qualitative research approach with descriptive, explanatory, and propositional scope was employed, supported by a systematic review of scientific literature, documentary analysis, and the conceptual design of the Panamanian People Analytics and Artificial Intelligence Maturity Model (MPM-PAIA). The findings indicate that organizations with greater analytical capabilities improve strategic decision-making, strengthen the efficiency of human resource processes, and enhance competitiveness. Data quality, leadership, organizational culture, analytical competencies, and ethical governance were identified as critical success factors. The study concludes that the progressive integration of People Analytics and Artificial Intelligence represents a strategic opportunity for Panamanian organizations, provided that technological adoption is accompanied by workforce development and ethical governance.

items.title: Transformational Leadership in Building a Culture of Artificial Intelligence Utilization in Schools
items.abstract: The rise of generative artificial intelligence has changed teachers' professional work, yet its use in schools depends less on technology than on leadership that builds vision, competence, support, and a culture of responsible use. Using transformational leadership theory as a lens, this study analyzes how a foundation head builds a culture of artificial intelligence utilization in a school and how the dimensions of transformational leadership appear in that process. A qualitative single case study was conducted at an Islamic elementary school in Pekanbaru, Indonesia. Data were collected on 26 August 2026 through interviews with five purposively selected teachers and the foundation head as the key informant, and were supported by observation and documentation. The data were analyzed through condensation, coding, categorization, theme development, and theoretical interpretation. The findings show that leadership operates through five interrelated mechanisms: vision and role modeling, capacity building, social learning, responsible use, and institutionalization. The foundation head demonstrated artificial intelligence use personally, organized structured training, provided facilities, encouraged peer exchange, and insisted on verifying outputs. Teachers used these tools for lesson plans, materials, assessments, and media, and practice appears to be moving from individual adoption toward institutionalized routines, although this conclusion remains tentative given the limited scope of the study. The novelty of this study is the Artificial Intelligence Transformational Leadership Pathway, a conceptual model that sequentially links the four dimensions of transformational leadership to collective norms of technology use.

Particular attention is paid to the pedagogical benefits, practical challenges, and ethical considerations associated with the implementation of these technologies. The article argues that successful digital transformation requires not only technological innovation but also pedagogically grounded implementation, teacher training, digital literacy, and responsible use of AI.

items.abstract: This article explores the challenges of translating Uzbek literary texts into English by comparing Shuhrat Sattorov’s English translation of Shukur Kholmirzaev’s short story “The Character of the Uzbeks” with translations produced by artificial intelligence tools. The main purpose is to identify common translation errors and examine how AI handles the linguistic, cultural, and contextual features of the original text. Special attention is given to the translation of culture-specific expressions, words with multiple meanings, sentence structures, and elements that reflect Uzbek national identity. By comparing the selected translations, the study aims to show where AI can provide clear and useful translations and where it may fail to preserve the writer’s intended meaning and cultural message.

items.title: Turkish Adaptation and Psychometric Properties of the Trust in Artificial Intelligence Based Educational Technologies Scale
items.abstract: The rapid spread of artificial intelligence-based technologies has made trust a fundamental element in the sustainable adoption of these technologies. This study aimed to adapt the Artificial Intelligence-Based Educational Technologies Trust Scale developed by Nazaretsky et al. (2022b) into Turkish in the context of prospective teachers and to examine its psychometric validity and reliability. Data were collected from 423 undergraduate students enrolled in various programs at a state university. The factor structure of the scale was analyzed using confirmatory factor analysis (CFA). The fit indices of the initial 25-item model fell below acceptable thresholds. Repeated analyses resulted in a three-factor, 21-item solution. This final structure is consistent with the original dimensions, named Perceived Benefits, Perceived Barriers/Concerns, and Trust in AI-Based Educational Technologies. The fit indices for the final model were found to be acceptable (e.g., χ2/df = 1.425, RMSEA = 0.052, SRMR = 0.061). The Cronbach's alpha internal consistency coefficient for the entire scale was calculated as 0.803. The Cronbach's alpha coefficients for the subscales were 0.813, 0.684, and 0.811, respectively. Convergent and discriminant validity analyses showed that the scale is valid and reliable in its current form. These findings lay the groundwork for creating a standardized framework for monitoring and comparing trust in AI-based educational technologies among educators, policymakers, and researchers in Türkiye.
